Definitions, derivations, notes, and long tables start folded.

How Splashery is built

Everything else in this manual is about what a toy is. This chapter is about the program that holds the toys: where its files are, why it is made of plain files with no build step, what the PlayCanvas engine does for us, what we wrote ourselves, and every outside library that ships with the site. The file names are real. Open the source beside this page and you can follow along.

Plain files, and nothing else

Splashery is static files and ES modules. There is no bundler (nothing turns many files into one), no server program, no database, no content delivery network, and no key to a paid service. A web page asks for index.html; that page asks for src/app.js; and the browser follows each import line to the next file, one request each. The site is served as it sits in the repository (GitHub Pages serves the main branch), and to run it on your own computer you start any file server in the folder, for example python3 -m http.server 4173 --bind 127.0.0.1. There is nothing to install first, and package.json has no build step.

Why this way? No bundler, no server

Our choice It is a ground rule of the project (CLAUDE.md), kept on purpose.

Four things follow from it. A toy can be read: the file you open in the browser's tools is the file in the repository, not a squeezed copy. The site costs nothing to run beyond free file hosting, and has no application server of its own that could fail. (The files still have to be served by some host, GitHub Pages today, or a file server on your own computer, and the page loads them over the network, so it can still be unreachable when the host or the network is down.) Your scenes and files stay on your device, because there is no server to send them to (the Terms of use in the About tab say so). And a page that embeds a toy (embed/index.html, the <splashery-toy> element in src/element.js) needs only a few static files, with a test that keeps an embed under 30 MB.

If it were chosen differently. A bundler would make the first load smaller and faster (one file instead of hundreds, with unused code removed). A server would allow short links, saved accounts, and heavy work done off the phone. Each costs something the four points above give for free. The cost of the choice today is that a rarely used part must be loaded by hand, only when its toy opens (see the libraries below).

Where it lives: index.html, package.json, playwright.config.mjs (the test server is the same file server), and CLAUDE.md (the ground rules).

Where the files are

Folder or file What is in it
index.html, styles.css The app: one page, its styles, and a small import map for the GIF encoder.
src/ The program. The core is a few files: app.js and ui.js (wiring and panels), player.js (the clock, camera, effects, and tools for the toy on show), stage.js (the one place that talks to the engine), state.js and codec.js (the scene document and the link; see "Share links and QR codes"), toys.js (the shelf), and kit.js with generators.js (the toy kit, Chapter 2).
src/packs/ The toys' recipes, one file for each family of toys (about a hundred files): balls.js, food.js, splat-equation.js (the language of Chapter 3), and so on. A recipe is the JavaScript of Chapter 2; src/toys.js lists each toy with the pack it comes from and whether it is behind the labs switch.
src/arcade/, src/fluids/, src/physics/, src/qr/, src/live/, and other folders Bigger systems that more than one toy shares, each in its own folder: the games, the liquids and flames, the hands-on physics, QR codes, and the microphone and camera. Most are loaded only when a toy that needs them opens.
assets/ Captured toys (as .sog files), thumbnails, flags, and the sounds and data some toys read. Every asset's license is in CREDITS.md.
vendor/ Other people's libraries, copied in as they were published. Four needed a small change to load here (a comment removed, or a line added so the file loads as an ES module, or the TypeScript compiled to JavaScript); LICENSES.md records each one. The next two sections list them all.
tools/ Node scripts that run on a build machine and are never loaded by the site: they prepare assets, make thumbnails and clips, build the site's pages (tools/site-build.mjs), print this manual's PDF (tools/manual-pdf.mjs), and keep the plan of every toy (tools/toy-plan.json).
tests/ The Playwright tests, which open the real site in a real browser. For example, tests/taps.spec.mjs finds every toy's tap by itself, so a new toy is tried the day it is added.
embed/, worlds/, showcase/, site/, manual/, pdf-lab/ The other pages of the site: the embed player, the Worlds, the Showcase, the guides and Learn hub (site/), this manual, and the PDF lab.

What PlayCanvas does, and what is our own

PlayCanvas is an open source (MIT) web graphics engine. Splashery vendors version 2.22.3 as one file, vendor/playcanvas/playcanvas.min.mjs, and every other file reaches it only through src/pc.js, which does nothing but re-export it. The ordinary toys never touch it: src/stage.js (with src/paint.js and src/loaders.js) is the one place that sets up the device and shows a toy, and only about two dozen files in all (the stage, the fluids, the Worlds, the live relief, and a few toys that draw extra layers) import src/pc.js.

PlayCanvas does Our own code does
Opens the graphics device: WebGPU when the browser has a working one, otherwise WebGL2 (deviceOrder in src/stage.js picks). Says which to try first, shows a plain message when neither exists, and falls back to a poster.
Holds the splats in textures, projects each one to the screen (Chapter 1), draws it as a quad with a Gaussian falloff, and blends them back to front. Decides which splats exist: the kit and generators build them from recipes (src/kit.js, src/generators.js), and the equation language makes them from your formulas.
Sorts the splats by depth on a worker, a few frames after anything moves (the comment in src/stage.js about "splat sorting" is about this). Keeps frames coming while the sort finishes, and asks for a new sort when the toy moves.
Reads .sog and .ply splat files and runs a function on every splat each frame (a "work buffer modifier"). The modifier itself: the per-splat effects and the kit's parts, hinges, morphs, and colors, written in two shader languages (src/effects.js), plus the sharper falloff in src/kernels.js. Also reads .splat and .spz files (src/loaders.js).
The scene graph, a camera, and a loop that calls us each frame. The orbit camera and touch gestures (src/camera.js), paint (src/paint.js), picking, sound (src/sound.js, WebAudio), the panels, the scene document, and every toy.

So the engine is the drawing machine, and the toys are ours. Splashery is primarily splat based, not only: the photo toys' Sharp view is a textured mesh of triangles (src/live/relief-mesh.js), the WebGPU liquid surface and the gas grid are extra passes drawn after the splats (src/fluids/gpu/), and the hands-on physics and the games' rules are ordinary JavaScript with no drawing in them at all. (See "What else Splashery does now".)

Where it lives: src/pc.js (the one import), src/stage.js (the device, the toy's entity, the sort), src/effects.js and src/kernels.js (the shader code), vendor/playcanvas/LICENSE.

Every library that ships, and when it loads

These are all the outside libraries and models in vendor/, the only files in the site that we did not write. LICENSES.md has the full notice and source for each. The rule (see CLAUDE.md) is that a library is vendored, loaded only when the toy that needs it opens, and listed there before it is used. Nothing is fetched from a content delivery network or an outside server, and no key is needed.

Library (folder in vendor/) Its job License When it loads
PlayCanvas 2.22.3 (playcanvas) The drawing engine, above. MIT With every page that draws a toy (the app, the embed, the Worlds).
gifenc 1.0.3 (gifenc) Writes an animated GIF when you export one. MIT With the app (src/exports.js imports it through the import map in index.html); it is small.
PDF.js 6.3.289 (pdfjs) Reads a PDF so its pages can become splats. Apache-2.0 (its image decoders: BSD and MIT) Only when you open a PDF (src/media.js).
omggif 1.0.10 (omggif) Reads a GIF's frames in browsers that cannot decode them (Safari). MIT Only when you open a GIF in such a browser.
ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0 (onnxruntime-web) Runs a neural network on your device, in WebAssembly. MIT Only when you open a photo or start a camera for depth, or a recording in Note Rider.
Depth Anything V2 Small, int8 (depth-anything-v2-small, about 27 MB) The model that guesses how far away each part of a photo is. Apache-2.0 Only when a toy needs depth (Photo to 3D and its relatives).
Basic Pitch model (basic-pitch, about 230 KB) The model that finds the notes in a recording. Apache-2.0 Only when you open a recording as your own song in Note Rider.
Splat.js 0.1.0 (splatjs) Trains a splat scene from the frames of a video. MIT Only when you open a video in Video to 3D (labs).
Project Nayuki's QR Code generator (qrcodegen) Writes the QR code's modules. MIT Only when something needs a code drawn: the QR code toy, the Share tab's scene code, or Save PDF (labs).
jsQR 1.4.0 (jsqr) Reads a QR code back, to check that it scans. Apache-2.0 Only when a code is read back and the browser's own barcode reader is not used or cannot read it. The QR code toy asks for jsQR directly, and so does the check that Save PDF runs on its code; the Share tab's scene code uses the browser's reader first and falls back to jsQR.
ZXing for JavaScript 0.21.3 (zxing-js) Writes and reads Data Matrix and Aztec codes. Apache-2.0 Only when the "Other barcodes" toy opens (labs).
pdf-lib 1.17.1 (pdf-lib) Writes a PDF when you choose Save PDF. MIT Only when you save a PDF from the Share tab (labs).
laz-perf 0.0.7 (laz-perf) Reads a .laz point cloud. Apache-2.0 Only when you open a .laz file in Point clouds (labs).
dicom-parser 1.8.21 (dicom-parser) Reads a DICOM medical scan. MIT Only when you open a DICOM file in the Volume viewer (labs).
libwebp, from splat-transform 3.6.1 (webp) Reads and writes the lossless pictures inside a .sog file. MIT and BSD-3-Clause Only when you open or save a .sog in the Splat toolkit (labs).

The Wikipedia book, the earthquakes toy, and the molecule viewer's fetch by Protein Data Bank code do read from outside the site while you use it, but they fetch data (an article, a feed, a structure), not code, only when you ask, and a dated snapshot of the earthquake feed ships for when it cannot be reached. The white stork migration is not one of them: it reads a data file that ships with the site. The outside download of that data happens earlier, when a tool in tools/ builds the file on a build machine, not in your browser.

What is used to build the site, but is not in it

package.json lists pinned devDependencies (the Playwright test runner, Prettier, a splat converter, glTF readers, and the QR readers used to test codes). Some programs outside npm (Blender, the Brush and msplat trainers) make the captured splats on a build machine. None of them is served; LICENSES.md, under "Development tools" and "Build tools outside npm", lists each with its license.

How a toy gets on the shelf

Putting this together: a toy is a recipe in a file in src/packs/, one entry in src/toys.js (its id, label, category, pack, and whether it is labs), its sound in src/toy-sounds.js, its help text in src/toy-help.js, and its plan in tools/toy-plan.json. Nothing is compiled or registered anywhere else. The next time the page loads, the toy is on the shelf, and the tests find it.

Where it lives: README.md ("Layout"), LICENSES.md, CREDITS.md, docs/PACKS.md (how to write a recipe).
